what: Protosynthex I (Simmons, System Development Corporation) answered English questions typed as punched cards by searching a full index of the Golden Book Encyclopedia
fit: A computer holding encyclopedic text answered free English questions put to it, matching the broad-knowledge, ordinary-language definition (mechanism: index lookup and matching, not deep understanding).

sources.title: DTIC AD0414777 (Protosynthex report)
sources.quote: Protosynthex I, accepts ordinary text and English questions as its inputs.

sources.title: DTIC AD0414777 (Protosynthex report)
sources.quote: a complete index of the Golden Book Encyclopedia was made and this text serves as the basis for the question-answering system

note: Replaces the second pass's 1993 START. Earlier candidates: BASEBALL (1961) and similar early question answerers answered only within one narrow database (baseball statistics), so rejected as not broad knowledge. Protosynthex's source was a children's encyclopedia, so breadth is modest but it is open-domain. Later: START 1993, Ask Jeeves 1996, Watson 2011.
searched: Leads file (Protosynthex quotes re-checked with page_text3 --check: FOUND); ia_search3 for START/Boris Katz 1993-1997 and Siri 2011-2012; Wikipedia Boris Katz, Siri, Ask.com pages.

what: MIT's START went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions from the public on many topics (Boris Katz)
fit: A publicly reachable computer answering ordinary-language factual questions on many topics, used by outside people for that purpose; knowledge is hand-annotated so breadth is limited.

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

note: Kept from the second pass. No earlier deployed open-domain question answerer was found (Protosynthex was a research system). Ask Jeeves 1996 is later and matched questions to pages. No contemporary 1993-1995 source found in ia_search3.
searched: ia_search3 'START' 'Boris Katz' 1993-1997 (only a 1993 book snippet that says Katz invited journalists to use START; not fetched/quoted); Wikipedia Boris Katz and Ask.com.

what: Apple's Siri, integrated into the iPhone 4S at its release on 14 October 2011, put spoken question answering in millions of ordinary users' hands
fit: A consumer device that answers ordinary-language factual questions (e.g. how tall is Mount Everest) for everyday users; knowledge is drawn from web services such as Wikipedia.

sources.title: Siri
sources.quote: integrated it into the iPhone 4s at its release on October 14, 2011

note: Earlier: Ask Jeeves (1996) accepted natural-language questions but returned page links, not answers. Later: Alexa/Google Assistant 2014-2016. Date is a judgement of when answering by voice became routine.
searched: Wikipedia Siri and Ask.com; ia_search3 Siri 2011-2012 (only book/newspaper mentions).

concept_note: Changed first_demonstration from START 1993 to Protosynthex I 1963 (open-domain encyclopedia question answering, contemporary DTIC source). START 1993 moved to first_practical_use; added mass_adoption Siri 2011. BASEBALL 1961 rejected as narrow-domain.

what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touch display for computer input/output (air traffic control) in Electronics Letters
fit: A transparent capacitive screen over a display let a user control a computer by touching the screen with a finger, matching the touch-screen mechanism.

sources.title: Touch display - a novel input/output device for computers
sources.quote: Touch display—a novel input/output device for computers

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

note: Confirms the second pass, now with a contemporary source (Crossref record dated 1965-10; only the title is quotable). Rejected earlier: Philco 1946 and AT&T Harmon 1962 stylus/light-beam patents (patents, not shown working), 1963 light-pen patent (pointing device, not touch). Gesture and glove side: nothing earlier (Sayre Glove 1977, theremin is an instrument).
searched: Crossref for Johnson 1965; Wikipedia Touchscreen; WebSearch on Johnson ATC use (only blogs; no operational date).

what: PLATO IV terminals at the University of Illinois (1972) had a built-in 16x16 infrared touch panel that students used to answer questions in lessons
fit: Students controlled a teaching computer by touching its screen, a touch-panel input used for its real purpose (instruction) outside the lab.

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Touch panel: A 16×16 grid infrared touch panel, allowing students to answer questions by touching anywhere on the screen.

sources.title: ERIC ED084845
sources.quote: Touch-panel: Senses the presence of ihe student's finger or another object as it nears the plasma-panel

note: Same as the second pass (replaced CERN 1973). The December 1972 handout describes the PLATO IV touch panel and says Northwestern's terminal arrives January 1973, so 1972-73 is the window; the 1972 start rests on Wikipedia. Johnson's ATC display (1965-68) appears to have stayed experimental; sources found place its operational ATC use much later. Telefunken 1970 was a patent/prototype.
searched: ia_search3 'touch panel' PLATO 1972-1975; Wikipedia Touchscreen and PLATO; WebSearch Johnson operational ATC use.

what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone
fit: Ordinary consumers used finger touch to control their phones routinely.

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

note: Kept from the second pass; date is a judgement within 2007-2010. ATM/kiosk touchscreens (1980s-90s), HP-150 (1983), IBM Simon (1993) and Nintendo DS (2004) were niche or limited.

concept_note: Confirmed all three second-pass milestones; added a contemporary Crossref source for Johnson 1965 and a Dec 1972 ERIC source for the PLATO IV touch panel. Gesture/glove side offers nothing earlier.

what: MowBot, a rechargeable electric lawn mower that steered itself around the lawn and stopped at obstructions, advertised and sold by MOWBOT Inc. (Tonawanda, NY; S. L. Bellinger)
fit: A small self-guided machine that mows a lawn on its own, matching the definition; the 1959 Whirlpool track-following sweeper was rejected as it did not navigate on its own.

sources.title: House & Garden, May 1969
sources.quote: Electronically-controlled MOWBOT mows and steers itself around your lawn until the grass is completely cut.

sources.title: Life, 19 September 1969
sources.quote: Mowbot does avoid all per- manent obstacles such as trees, flower beds, etc.

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger

note: Replaces the second pass's 1959 Whirlpool demo: that concept followed a track and was a concept demonstration, a loose fit to 'on its own', so no earlier strictly fitting demo is claimed. No earlier robot mower or vacuum found (searched 1945-1968 magazines, no hits). Later: Trilobite 1996-97, Roomba 2002. Demonstration and practical use are the same event as no earlier prototype report was found.
searched: ia_search3 'automatic lawn mower' 1945-1968 and robot lawn mower in Popular Science (0 hits), Whirlpool/Moscow 1958-60 (irrelevant hits); Wikipedia Robotic vacuum cleaner and lawn mower; leads re-checked FOUND.

what: MowBot went on sale to the public in 1969 (about $800), first commercial autonomous lawn mower
fit: Customers used the machine for its real purpose, mowing lawns without being driven.

sources.title: House & Garden, May 1969
sources.quote: Electronically-controlled MOWBOT mows and steers itself around your lawn until the grass is completely cut.

sources.title: Robotic lawn mower
sources.quote: In 1969, the MowBot was introduced and patented by S Lawrence Bellinger

note: Confirms the second pass. The advertisement shows it offered for sale in 1969; no sales figures found, and how well it worked is unverified. Electrolux Trilobite (1996/2001) and Roomba (2002) are later.

what: iRobot's Roomba (debut September 2002) had sold over two million units by late 2006, in millions of homes
fit: A small autonomous floor-cleaning robot used routinely by ordinary households.

sources.title: SERVO Magazine, November 2006
sources.quote: is the run-away best selling "home robot" ever, with over two million sold and counting

note: New kind (the second pass had none). Roomba launched 2002 and was the first commercially successful robot vacuum; 'common' is a judgement, and 2005-2007 is plausible. Trilobite 1996 failed in the market.
searched: SERVO Magazine Nov 2006 via archive.org; Wikipedia Robotic vacuum cleaner.

concept_note: Moved first_demonstration from Whirlpool 1959 (track-following concept, loose fit) to MowBot 1969, now with contemporary ads; kept practical use 1969; added mass_adoption from Roomba sales (2006). No robot vacuum earlier than 1996 found.
